name: Zimbabwe Birds
what: Eight soapstone birds, each about 40 cm tall on a column, carved at Great Zimbabwe between the 13th and 15th centuries. One is on Zimbabwe's flag.
why: Colonial collectors carried them off as proof of a lost non-African civilisation, a myth used to justify Rhodesia. Bringing them home became part of Zimbabwe's independence.
now: Seven are in Zimbabwe, mostly at the Great Zimbabwe site museum; one is still at Groote Schuur, Cecil Rhodes's house in Cape Town.

sources.cite: Matenga, E. (1998). The Soapstone Birds of Great Zimbabwe: Symbols of a Nation. African Publishing Group.
Garlake, P. (1973). Great Zimbabwe. Thames & Hudson.

stops.note: Carved for the hill complex and the eastern enclosure of Great Zimbabwe, the capital of a gold-trading state of the 13th-15th centuries. They may stand for royal ancestors.
stops.meet: a stone carver of Great Zimbabwe

stops.note: The hunter Willi Posselt cut one bird from its column in 1889 and sold it to Cecil Rhodes, who kept it in his house and adopted it as an emblem.
A German missionary sold the lower half of another bird to the Berlin museum.
Taken by the Red Army from Berlin at the end of the Second World War; it returned to Germany decades later.
After independence South Africa returned four birds taken in the 1890s, in an exchange of museum collections. The Rhodes bird stayed at Groote Schuur.
The Berlin fragment came home in 2003 and was reunited with the top half of its bird.
stops.meet: a visitor at the Great Zimbabwe museum
